advice: Don't trust a single energy reading of code that runs in under a millisecond.
detail: Hardware counters like Intel RAPL update roughly every 1 ms. Sub-millisecond workloads showed over 110% variation and often read zero.

advice: To measure a tiny function, run it many times in a loop and divide the total energy by the count.
detail: PowerLens repeats each code block 1,000 times so its energy rises above the counter's resolution.

advice: Lock the CPU frequency, disable Turbo Boost, pin to one core and stop background jobs before benchmarking energy.
detail: Frequency scaling and other processes otherwise leak into your readings.

advice: Repeat each energy measurement about 10 times, drop the outliers, and report the mean.
detail: With 10 trials and IQR outlier removal, over 90% of code blocks varied by less than 10% between trials.

advice: Let the hardware cool down between benchmark runs, and average across repetitions.
detail: HarmonE's experiments used five repetitions with a 20-minute cooldown between runs to keep hardware conditions stable.

advice: Sanity-check fine-grained energy numbers by confirming they add up to a whole-program measurement.
detail: Summed block-level readings closely matched whole-program energy, with much lower variance.

advice: Compare relative energy trends, not absolute joules, across different machines or measurement tools.
detail: Software meters like pyRAPL give Intel-specific estimates, so absolute values shift between platforms.

advice: Subtract an idle baseline and the model server's own energy to see what your framework really costs.
detail: The study records a 60-second idle reading per machine and tracks the model-serving process separately to isolate framework overhead.

advice: Use runtime and output tokens as quick proxies for an agent's energy; memory use tells you little.
detail: Energy correlated strongly with duration (R = 0.89) and output tokens (R = 0.88). Memory showed near-zero correlation because it is allocated upfront.

advice: Log LLM call counts and input/output tokens next to every energy reading.
detail: The volume of reasoning tokens can inflate energy independently of how well a framework orchestrates its work.

advice: Look at loop-heavy and deeply nested blocks first when hunting for energy hotspots.
detail: Loop count, conditionals, nesting and cognitive complexity all correlate with block energy across 18,000+ Python programs. Each link is weak on its own, so treat them as signals to check, not verdicts.

advice: Give blocks dense with arithmetic and other operators a closer look for energy cost.
detail: Operator density was the top-ranked feature in all three of EnCoDe's tree-based prediction models.

advice: Don't use cyclomatic complexity or code size alone as a stand-in for energy cost.
detail: Complexity metrics alone predicted energy tiers at 51% accuracy, which is barely above chance. Energy depends on how code features combine.

advice: Use static energy estimation to shortlist hotspots before you run anything, then confirm by measuring.
detail: Models trained on 33 static code features sorted blocks into low, medium or high energy with 80.6% accuracy. They're built for ranking hotspots, not exact joules.

advice: When refactoring a flagged block, compare the estimated energy of the old and new versions.
detail: EnCoDe's workflow flags high-energy blocks, then gives a comparative estimate between the original and refactored code to guide the choice.

advice: Keep your energy-analysis tooling lightweight too.
detail: A Gradient Boosting classifier used 0.015 J against Random Forest's 0.373 J for nearly identical accuracy (78.8% vs 79.2%).

advice: Compare agent frameworks on energy before adopting one; the architecture alone can swing usage 9×.
detail: On the same model and hardware, AutoCodeRover used 9.4× more energy per run than OpenHands.

advice: Track energy per successfully completed task, not per run.
detail: Small-model agents resolved almost no issues, so most of the energy they consumed bought nothing.

advice: Add loop detection: stop or change strategy when an agent repeats the same failing action.
detail: Small models kept resubmitting the same failing test script or malformed API call, and the frameworks never noticed.

advice: Filter and trim tool output before it reaches the model's context window.
detail: Broad grep commands returned huge unfiltered outputs that overwhelmed a 32K context and caused the agent to lose track.

advice: Never trust an agent's own "success" report; gate every generated patch on CI builds and tests.
detail: Frameworks reported success for destructive patches, such as replacing a 2,000-line file with a single invalid line.

advice: Treat suspiciously low agent energy as a possible early failure, not efficiency.
detail: Some low-energy runs ended early when the prompt exceeded the model's token limit, before any real work began.

advice: Budget for the orchestration loop, not just the model calls.
detail: Planning, memory, tool, reflection and retry cycles burn energy on every iteration, and agents often run for minutes or hours.

advice: Scan an agent framework's TODO, FIXME and HACK comments before betting production on it.
detail: Prior work found ML projects carry twice the self-admitted technical debt of non-ML projects. This study tests whether that debt also tracks energy use.

advice: Pin agent framework versions and re-measure energy after every upgrade.
detail: These frameworks change quickly, which is why the study compares releases several months apart.

advice: Prefer agent frameworks you can run locally and instrument; you can't optimise energy you can't observe.
detail: Observability and local deployability were selection criteria for the frameworks in the study.

advice: Keep a range of light to heavy models, and serve the lightest one that meets your accuracy target.
detail: HarmonE kept 95% of the heavy model's accuracy using 45.5% of its energy, and cut inference time by 53%.

advice: Check the energy cost of each candidate model before defaulting to the most accurate one.
detail: An LSTM reached R² 0.917 against an SVM's 0.821 for traffic forecasting, but used about 8.4× the energy.

advice: Benchmark energy across model sizes; the largest variant may cost 4× for a marginal gain.
detail: YOLOv8m used about 4.3× the energy of YOLOv8n for a 0.05 rise in mean detection confidence.

advice: Don't drop a small model into an agent framework built for large ones and expect savings.
detail: Swapping a small model in for a large one was found to be ineffective and often counterproductive. Current frameworks assume a capable reasoning engine.

advice: A smaller model can use more energy inside an agent loop; measure, don't assume.
detail: In two of four frameworks, Qwen-3 1.7B burned more tokens and energy than the larger Gemma-3 4B.

advice: Judge local models on total cost of ownership, not just the missing API bill.
detail: Local runs avoided API fees but some configurations averaged 24 to 27 minutes per issue.

advice: Retrain when data drift is detected, not on a fixed timer.
detail: Drift-triggered retraining used 54.5% less energy than an LSTM retrained on a fixed schedule.

advice: Before scheduling regular retraining of a heavy model, check that the accuracy gain is worth the energy.
detail: Periodic retraining added about 38% more energy to an LSTM for a gain of just 0.008 R².

advice: Store each model with the data distribution it was trained on, and reuse it when those conditions return.
detail: HarmonE checks its model repository for a matching past model before retraining, avoiding redundant work when familiar patterns recur.

advice: Pair model switching with selective retraining; switching alone drifts toward the heaviest model.
detail: Switch-only used more energy than HarmonE (24.3 vs 20.6 mJ) and still fell short of the heavy model's accuracy.

advice: Let the system adapt models to runtime conditions instead of always running the heaviest one.
detail: Adaptive operation kept about 97.5% of a static LSTM's accuracy with roughly 44% less energy.

advice: Set measurable accuracy, energy and drift thresholds at design time, and let them trigger actions.
detail: HarmonE turns sustainability goals into concrete limits, such as a maximum data-drift score before retraining.

advice: Monitor energy alongside accuracy and data drift in production, not accuracy alone.
detail: HarmonE's monitor combines accuracy, normalised energy and drift into one view of system health.

advice: Smooth your metrics and use tolerance bands so brief spikes don't trigger costly adaptations.
detail: HarmonE made 12 adaptations, against 17 for switching with periodic retraining.

advice: Don't let overhead worries stop you; a lightweight monitor-and-adapt loop costs very little.
detail: HarmonE's adaptation loop accounted for just 1.37% of total energy use.

advice: Keep adaptation logic in a separate control layer, outside your training and inference code.
detail: Harmonica wraps existing ML pipelines with an adaptation loop without changing how they train or serve.

advice: Store thresholds and adaptation policies in editable config, not hard-coded values.
detail: Harmonica keeps policies in JSON files that can be updated through a dashboard or API at runtime.

advice: Show energy and accuracy live against their thresholds so trade-offs are visible.
detail: Participants in Harmonica's user study named live telemetry the tool's strongest feature.

advice: Log every adaptation decision next to inference results so you can audit trade-offs later.
detail: Harmonica keeps historical logs of inference results and adaptation events for later analysis.
